meta.note: One real (synthetic) flagged exemplar per integrity family. Peer z-scores, the composite decomposition, rule thresholds and signature views are the live pipeline’s — no PII or card numbers. Decision-support indicators, not final determinations.

edu.tagline: A benign category code hiding a riskier line of business.
edu.definition: A merchant registers under a low-risk category code, but actually sells something riskier — gambling, adult, pharma — that the bank would have priced differently or refused outright.
edu.analogy: A late-night casino operating behind a shopfront licensed as a ‘gift shop’.
mechanic: Apply for card acceptance under a boring, low-risk category code (e.g. 5999 misc. retail).
Route the real, higher-risk product through that clean shell.
Behaviour — hours, channel, geography, declines — follows the true business, not the declared one.
Collect the lighter scrutiny, lower fees and smaller reserves the true category would never get.
edu.cost: The acquiring bank under-priced the risk and eats the chargebacks; card networks levy miscoding fines; an illegal true vertical adds regulatory and reputational exposure.
edu.legitTwin: A genuine specialty retailer resembles none of the prohibited verticals — a miscoder lights up several at once. That concurrency is the tell.

tells.why: Booked between 11pm and 5am — a gambling/adult rhythm, not a retailer’s.
An exact round number — people rarely buy goods at precisely $60.00.
Card-not-present — no physical card, unusual for the declared shopfront.
Settled through an acquirer in a third country the declared business never needs.
Refused by the issuer — often because the true product isn’t permitted.

rules.name: descriptor_churn_rule
rules.label: Descriptor churn
rules.plain: The billing name changes repeatedly to unrelated words — resetting dispute monitoring.

rules.name: dispute_excursion_rule
rules.label: Dispute excursion
rules.plain: Chargebacks and refunds run far above any healthy merchant.

rules.name: issuer_prohibition_rule
rules.label: Issuer prohibition declines
rules.plain: Issuers keep declining the true product as ‘not permitted’ despite a clean code.

edu.tagline: The right business, coded into a cheaper interchange band than it deserves.
edu.definition: The merchant is roughly in the right business, but is coded into a cheaper interchange band than its behaviour warrants — underpaying network fees on every sale.
edu.analogy: Shipping freight but labelling every pallet ‘documents’ to get the cheaper letter rate.
mechanic: Get assigned — or negotiate into — a lower interchange band than the behaviour qualifies for.
Flag transactions to hold the cheap rate: mark card-not-present as card-present, one-off as recurring.
Pocket the few basis points of difference across millions of dollars in volume.
edu.cost: The network and the acquirer are systematically underpaid; the issuer is under-compensated for the risk it carries. Audits claw back the shortfall and add assessments.
edu.legitTwin: A legitimate merchant’s declared band matches its behaviour. Here the paid rate sits tens of basis points below the band the behaviour actually warrants.

tells.why: Card-not-present — no physical card, unusual for the declared shopfront.
Tagged ‘recurring’ to qualify for a cheaper interchange band.
Flagged card-present, but the channel says card-not-present — a rate-qualification trick.

rules.name: interchange_abuse_rule
rules.label: Interchange abuse
rules.expr: interchange advantage > 50bps on a cheap band, or CNP-mismatch > 0.55
rules.plain: The rate actually paid sits well below the band the behaviour warrants.

edu.tagline: One purchase chopped into bursts to slip under an authorization ceiling.
edu.definition: A single purchase is deliberately split into several smaller charges within minutes, so each fragment stays under an authorization ceiling the whole would have tripped.
edu.analogy: Buying a $2,000 TV as ten separate $200 gift-cards to dodge the ‘manager approval over $500’ rule.
mechanic: The real ticket would exceed an auth floor, a review threshold or a no-signature ceiling.
The terminal rings it as several back-to-back charges on the same card.
Each fragment auto-approves under the ceiling; the aggregate never gets a single-transaction review.
edu.cost: Bypasses the issuer’s per-transaction risk controls, so fraud and disputes the ceiling was meant to stop land on the issuer; the acquirer eats chargebacks and limit-avoidance fines.
edu.legitTwin: Legitimate splits (deposit + balance, partial shipment) are spaced out. Abuse is dense in time and hugs the ceiling — that combination is the tell.

tells.why: Sits just below a round authorization ceiling — a split-ticket fragment.
Part of a same-card burst of charges moments apart.
An exact round number — people rarely buy goods at precisely $60.00.

rules.name: split_ticketing_rule
rules.label: Split-ticket burst
rules.plain: Many charges cluster just under an authorization ceiling, moments apart on one card.

verdict.behavesAs: one purchase split into sub-ceiling bursts

edu.tagline: One registered account secretly settling for a network of hidden sellers.
edu.definition: A registered merchant runs other, undisclosed businesses’ card sales through its own account — the bank thinks it is paying one shop but is settling for a hidden network.
edu.analogy: A licensed market stall quietly renting its till to a dozen unlicensed vendors.
mechanic: A merchant with a clean, approved account lends its ID to third parties who couldn’t get their own.
Those sub-merchants’ sales are injected into the host’s settlement stream.
Descriptors, geographies and volume suddenly diverge from the host’s declared business.
edu.cost: The acquirer onboards un-vetted, unknown sellers blind — absorbing their chargebacks and unknowingly laundering their proceeds, with the AML/BSA liability that carries.
edu.legitTwin: Legitimate marketplaces and payment facilitators disclose their sub-merchants. Factoring hides them — the plurality of undisclosed identities is the tell.

tells.why: Carries a sub-merchant ID — a hidden third party settling through this account.
Settled through an acquirer in a third country the declared business never needs.
An unusually large, clean ticket — the shape of a cash withdrawal, not a sale.

rules.name: descriptor_churn_rule
rules.label: Descriptor churn
rules.plain: The billing name changes repeatedly to unrelated words — resetting dispute monitoring.

verdict.behavesAs: a settlement hub for undisclosed sellers

edu.tagline: A checkout card fee the rules don’t allow — over the cap, on debit/prepaid, or hidden.
edu.definition: The merchant adds a surcharge to card payments that breaks the brand rules: above the cost-of-acceptance cap, on debit or prepaid cards where it’s prohibited, or with no disclosure at the till. Cardholders don’t recognise the extra charge and dispute it as unauthorised.
edu.analogy: A shop that quietly adds a ‘card fee’ bigger than the law allows and never puts up a sign — so customers only find out on their statement.
mechanic: Surcharging is permitted only up to the merchant’s cost of acceptance, never on debit/prepaid, and only if disclosed.
This merchant applies a fee past the cap and onto prohibited cards, undisclosed at the point of sale.
The unexpected fee drives ‘I don’t recognise this’ disputes, chargebacks and fee reversals.
edu.cost: Cardholders pay a fee they never agreed to; issuers field the disputes; the acquirer carries a merchant breaching the network surcharge rules.
edu.legitTwin: A compliant merchant surcharges at or below its cost of acceptance, exempts debit/prepaid, and discloses the fee — so it doesn’t generate a wave of unexpected-fee disputes.

tells.why: Card-not-present — the surcharge is applied online where disclosure is easiest to skip.
Disputed / reversed — cardholders reject a fee they didn’t recognise.
The surcharge lifts an otherwise clean ticket by an odd, unexpected amount.

rules.name: surcharge_over_cap_rule
rules.label: Over-cap / prohibited surcharge
rules.plain: A card surcharge is applied above the cost-of-acceptance cap or on prohibited debit/prepaid cards.

verdict.behavesAs: a merchant surcharging cards over the brand cap

edu.tagline: Card acceptance used as an unlicensed cash-out channel.
edu.definition: The merchant uses card acceptance to hand out cash — effectively an unlicensed ATM — dodging the cash-advance fees and AML scrutiny a real cash business carries.
edu.analogy: A ‘gift shop’ whose register only ever rings up neat $200 and $500 ‘purchases’ and hands back an envelope of cash.
mechanic: Charge a card and return most of the value as cash, keeping a fee.
Because it’s coded as retail, it dodges cash-advance interchange, cash-out limits and AML scrutiny.
Enables money laundering and converts stolen cards to untraceable cash.
edu.cost: The acquirer becomes an unknowing cash-out and laundering conduit (BSA/OFAC liability); interchange is under-collected; issuers absorb the stolen-card fraud that gets cashed out.
edu.legitTwin: Round-number pricing alone is innocent. Cash-out combines round hundreds with high tickets and none of retail’s texture — no shipping, no refunds, no variety.

tells.why: An exact round number — people rarely buy goods at precisely $60.00.
An unusually large, clean ticket — the shape of a cash withdrawal, not a sale.
Settled through an acquirer in a third country the declared business never needs.

rules.name: dispute_excursion_rule
rules.label: Dispute excursion
rules.plain: Chargebacks and refunds run far above any healthy merchant.
